newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq Kurd chief threatens to enlist Baghdad's aid.
newsitem.headline: Iraq Kurd chief threatens to enlist Baghdad's aid.

text.p: Kurdish chieftain Massoud Barzani on Thursday threatened to ask the Iraqi government for further help in his feud with a rival militia.
"If the Kurdish people are under hard pressure of the PUK," we will ask for help from Iraq," Barzani told a news conference at his headquarters near the northern town of Salahuddin.
Barzani's rivals, the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), have closed in this week on the city of Arbil, which Barzani's men captured with the backing of Iraqi tanks and troops in late August.
The Iraqi intervention in its northern Kurdish region prompted the United States to launch missiles at military targets in southern Iraq in reprisal.
Barzani's tough talk came ahead of a meeting in Turkey with a senior U.S. diplomat as part of a bid by Washington to end the Kurdish feud.
"Assistant Secretary of State Robert Pelletreau will come to Turkey tomorrow. He will meet us, and Massoud Barzani," a Turkish foreign ministry official told Reuters in Ankara.
Barzani repeated accusations that neighbouring Iran had supplied his rival group with munitions and around 13,000 men in a week-old offensive against him. Tehran denies the charges.
"If Iran has the right to support the PUK, why shouldn't we have the right to demand support from Iraq," he said.
There has been no sign of Iranian or Iraqi military presence on both sides of the Kurdish groups' lines in sporadic fighting this week.
Barzani said he was not willing to hold direct talks with PUK leader Jalal Talabani, despite the U.S. peace bid.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Wednesday that Pelletreau would soon meet Barzani and Talabani separately to "convince them that it is in their immediate interest to move towards a ceasefire and not to allow Iran or Iraq the opportunity to inflame the situation further."
A U.S.-led allied air force set up to shield the Kurds from Baghdad did not try to prevent President Saddam Hussein's forces entering Arbil. It has played no part in the Kurdish conflict.

"Our core, fundamental assessment is that neither of them can win militarily on the battlefield, but we believe that by stopping the fighting and agreeing at least to work together... they can restore stability to northern Iraq and hopefully keep Iran and Iraq out," Burns said.
U.S. defence officials said they had no evidence that elite Iraqi Republican Guard forces were moving north for fresh fighting as Talabani's Kurdish group had claimed.
"There is no movement. We do not see it," one said.
Talabani said he would not try to recapture Arbil, citing the presence of what he says is Iraqi armour there.

"We don't want to justify the interference of the Iraqi regime in the internal affairs of Iraqi Kurdistan and give a pretext to Iraq to fight again with Barzani," he told Reuters Television in his stronghold of Sulaimaniya.
But the PUK has taken two roads towards the city and some 6,000 Talabani fighters have gathered for a push near a third highway.
Senior PUK official Kosrat Rassoul said he and other leaders would meet later in the day to discuss whether to assault KDP positions around the city.
"The politburo is meeting this evening to make a decision on the attack," he said in the town of Koy Sanjak.
